title: At School
goal: Ask about a school, take part in a first-day introduction, and discuss a child's progress with a teacher.

runs.text: This chapter mainly gives a parent or caregiver's role. You may practice that role even if you do not have a child. Useful subjects include
English
math
science
history
art
music
, and
physical education
, often abbreviated
PE
. A
curriculum
describes what students study; a
class size
is the number of students in a class.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: We're considering this school. Could I ask a few questions?

turns.en: We're considering this school. Could I ask a few questions?

turns.speaker: Staff member

runs.text: Of course. What would you like to know?

turns.en: Of course. What would you like to know?

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: How many students are in each class?

turns.en: How many students are in each class?

turns.speaker: Staff member

runs.text: Twenty-two in this class.

turns.en: Twenty-two in this class.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: What after-school activities do you offer?

turns.en: What after-school activities do you offer?

turns.speaker: Staff member

runs.text: This term, we have art and soccer clubs.

turns.en: This term, we have art and soccer clubs.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: How do families find out about signing up?

turns.en: How do families find out about signing up?

turns.speaker: Staff member

runs.text: We'll give you the information for each club.

turns.en: We'll give you the information for each club.

blocks.caption: Asking about a school · Caregiver & Staff member

runs.text: The numbers and programs describe this fictional school. Other questions include
How much homework is assigned?
Is there an after-school program?
Do students wear a uniform?
, and
Who should I speak to about enrollment?
Enrollment
concerns joining as a student. Asking the relevant staff member lets you obtain the school's actual process.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: Hi, I'm Elena, Sam's aunt. Sam is starting today.

turns.en: Hi, I'm Elena, Sam's aunt. Sam is starting today.

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: Welcome, Sam. I'm Ms. Patel.

turns.en: Welcome, Sam. I'm Ms. Patel.

turns.speaker: Student

runs.text: Hi.

turns.en: Hi.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: He's excited, but a little nervous.

turns.en: He's excited, but a little nervous.

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: That's understandable. I'll show him where to put his bag.

turns.en: That's understandable. I'll show him where to put his bag.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: Thank you. Who should I contact if I have a question later?

turns.en: Thank you. Who should I contact if I have a question later?

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: The school office can direct you to the right person.

turns.en: The school office can direct you to the right person.

blocks.caption: A first day · Caregiver & Teacher & Student

runs.text: A little nervous
describes a feeling without saying the child cannot participate. A student can ask
Where should I put this?
or
Could you show me where to go?
These are supplied first-day support phrases, not an assumption that the student already knows every school instruction.

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: Sam is making progress in reading.

turns.en: Sam is making progress in reading.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: That's good to hear. How is he doing in math?

turns.en: That's good to hear. How is he doing in math?

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: He understands the ideas, but sometimes rushes through the work.

turns.en: He understands the ideas, but sometimes rushes through the work.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: Could you give me an example?

turns.en: Could you give me an example?

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: Yesterday, he skipped one part of an assignment.

turns.en: Yesterday, he skipped one part of an assignment.

turns.speaker: Caregiver

runs.text: What could we practice at home?

turns.en: What could we practice at home?

turns.speaker: Teacher

runs.text: We can agree on a small activity and check how it goes.

turns.en: We can agree on a small activity and check how it goes.

runs.text: How is he doing?
is a genuine progress question here, not simply a greeting.
Could you give me an example?
helps turn a broad report into something concrete. You can raise a concern yourself:
She's been worried about coming to school. Who can we talk to?
You can also disagree or request clarification:
That isn't what we're seeing at home. Could we compare notes?
For a solo route, read the staff or teacher lines and speak the caregiver's turns. Use the fictional facts in the models.
Ask about class size, an after-school program and enrollment information. The staff member offers to provide a leaflet; ask them to explain the enrollment section.
Introduce a child who is nervous on the first day. Ask who to contact with later questions.
The teacher says
She's doing well, but some assignments are unfinished.
Ask for an example and a possible next step.
Your concern is that the child is worried about school. State it and ask whom to speak to.
Sample possibilities:

“How many students are in a class? Could you explain the enrollment information?” / “This is Sam. He's a little nervous. Who should I contact with questions?” / “Could you give me an example? What could we work on?” / “She's worried about coming to school. Who can we talk to?”
Repeat later with a different subject or concern. Check that the questions invite specific information and that you did not have to invent a school rule to complete the exchange.
